title: Why You Sell Your Winners

beats.text: You'll sell your best stock, keep your worst, and feel smart doing it.
In the nineties, an economist studied seven years of trades from ten thousand accounts at a discount broker.
Meet Gary. He owns a rocket that's up and a dud that's down.
Gary needs cash. Which one goes?
A stock that was up was over fifty percent more likely to be sold.
So why dump the winner and hug the loser?
Worse, the winners they sold kept beating the losers they kept.
You see, it's like a late bus. The longer you wait, the harder it is to leave.
Selling the winner proves you were right. Selling the loser makes the mistake real.
Only one month flipped it: December.
Suddenly losers went first, because a loss sold before New Year can cut your tax bill.
Eleven months of pride. It took the taxman to make them admit it.

facts.claim: Odean analysed trading records of 10,000 accounts at a large (nationwide) discount brokerage house
Data covered January 1987 through December 1993 (seven years); paper published Journal of Finance 53(5), October 1998
A stock that is up in value is more than 50 percent more likely to be sold than one that is down (PGR 0.148 vs PLR 0.098 for the year)
The winners investors chose to sell continued to outperform the losers they kept; subsequent performance does not justify the behaviour
In December the pattern reverses (PLR 0.128 > PGR 0.108): tax-motivated selling of losses is most evident in December
Gary is a fictional illustrative investor, not a real person; the economist is not shown

caption:
Ten thousand real brokerage accounts, 1987 to 1993: a stock that was up was over 50% more likely to be sold than one that was down.
The winners they sold kept beating the losers they kept.
Only December flipped it. Taxes.
